package_info.package_manager: N/A (native Windows executables, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (modifies arbitrary native executables on affected systems)
package_info.why_malicious: Azov wiper is considered malicious because it injects destructive code into native Windows executables, irreversibly corrupting files and rendering systems inoperable. It masquerades as ransomware but offers no decryption or recovery mechanism, indicating its sole purpose is data destruction. The malware is designed to spread rapidly by infecting multiple executables, ensuring widespread and unrecoverable damage.

execution_context.trigger: When an infected executable is launched (runtime execution)
execution_context.file_location: Injected into native Windows executable files (.exe, .dll) located in system and user directories
required_permissions: filesystem (read/write/delete access to files and directories)
process execution (ability to run code within other executables)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When an infected executable is launched, the injected code enumerates files in target directories, overwrites the contents of executable files with random data, deletes non-executable files, and then terminates the process, resulting in irreversible destruction of user and system data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior is highly suspicious because legitimate software does not indiscriminately overwrite or delete large numbers of files, especially executables, without explicit user consent or a clear, documented purpose. The code operates autonomously and destructively upon execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal executables should not self-modify or corrupt other binaries, nor should they erase unrelated files. This code intentionally destroys data and system integrity, violating user trust and expected application behavior.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Secure file erasure tools may overwrite files for privacy, but only when explicitly invoked by the user and never by injecting into unrelated executables or operating without user interaction.
key_indicators: Injected code present in unrelated system and user executables
Mass overwriting of executable files with random data
Automated deletion of non-executable files in user and system directories
No recovery or decryption mechanism provided
Execution of destructive actions immediately upon process launch

attack_chain.action: Initial infection: Azov wiper is delivered and executed on the victim system, typically via malicious download or dropper.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is present and able to modify system files

attack_chain.action: Malicious payload injects code into native Windows executables (.exe, .dll) across system and user directories.
attack_chain.leads_to: Destructive payload is present in multiple system and user files

attack_chain.action: When an infected executable is launched, the injected code executes, enumerating files, overwriting executables with random data, and deleting non-executable files.
attack_chain.leads_to: Irreversible data destruction and system inoperability

behavioral_signatures: Unauthorized modification of native Windows executables (.exe, .dll) in system and user directories
Mass file overwriting with random or pseudo-random data patterns
Automated deletion of user and system files without user interaction
Presence of injected code that executes immediately upon process launch
Rapid, widespread file corruption events within a short time frame
file_indicators: Executable files with altered hashes not matching known-good versions
Presence of random or non-PE data in .exe/.dll files (file structure anomalies)
Sudden disappearance of user documents and executables from common directories (e.g., Desktop, Documents, Program Files)
Unexpected growth or corruption of executable file sizes
network_indicators: Typically none for Azov wiper (no command-and-control or data exfiltration observed)
May drop or display fake ransom notes locally to masquerade as ransomware, but no outbound network activity
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unauthorized or unexpected modifications to executable files, especially those with altered hashes or anomalous code sections. Alert on mass file overwriting or deletion events initiated by processes not associated with legitimate file erasure or update tools. Use endpoint protection to detect known Azov wiper signatures and behaviors, including the presence of injected code in system binaries. Correlate rapid, widespread file corruption or deletion with process ancestry to identify the source. Regularly compare file hashes of critical executables against known-good baselines.
